comparator.name: Computing Science (Informatica)
comparator.sourceNotes: The dated catalogue confirms 60 EC in each year. Year three has 30 EC of genuine electives, 12 EC of restricted choice and the 18 EC final project. Compiler Construction and Klassieke cryptografie are the first two of the three options. Standard project entry requires completion of years one and two, and direct entry follows at 144 EC with timely registration.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two coherent computing options are supported. The first concentrates on systems, algorithms and empirical evaluation, and the second emphasises mathematical modelling and intelligent systems. The other interests are represented within these programmes. A third option would lack a distinct, sustained course sequence.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both teach programming foundations. UCR develops structured Python programs, data collections and debugging.
Both develop logic, proofs and discrete structures for computing.
Both develop linear algebra through matrices, vectors, transformations and associated computational methods.
Both develop numerical approaches to scientific problems. UvA teaches these methods through a dedicated project.
Both develop statistical reasoning, probability and inference. UCR emphasises mathematical foundations and simulation.
Both teach data structures and algorithmic reasoning. UCR combines them in an advanced course.
Both analyse algorithm design and efficiency. UCR emphasises advanced algebraic and optimisation methods.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces the UvA automata and formal-languages component.
Both examine operating-system resource management. UCR combines operating systems and network foundations in one unit.
Both teach database design and queries. UCR focuses on relational databases.
Both develop software and evaluate its quality. UCR uses C++ and Haskell; UvA requires a dedicated large-team project.
Both consider societal and ethical questions about digital technology. UCR focuses on artificial intelligence.
UCR has no selected course equivalent to the historical and disciplinary survey Keerpunten in de Informatiewetenschappen.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces computer architecture and organization.
UCR has no selected dedicated web-technology course.

UCR Software Development includes C++ and Haskell, but that UCR course is already aligned to the stronger software-engineering counterpart; the separate UvA programming-languages requirement remains visible.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces the compulsory Internet of Things component.
UCR does not reproduce this separate computer-science-specific academic-skills component.
UCR Networks & Operating Systems includes networking, but is already aligned to the stronger operating-systems counterpart; UvA's separate networks-and-security requirement remains visible.
UCR has no selected course that reproduces distributed and parallel programming.

UCR has no selected compiler-construction course.
UCR has no selected cryptography course.
UCR teaches academic communication in broader courses. UvA provides separate computing-specific academic skills.
Both use mathematical and computational techniques to process and interpret digital images.
The genuine 30-EC open elective space is preserved without inventing a specific UvA minor or exchange curriculum.
UCR's optional independent-research opportunity is shown separately against this compulsory UvA bachelor project; it is not part of the fixed 180-EC UCR programme.

notes.text: UCR covers programming, databases, networks, operating systems, algorithms and visual computing. UvA also requires architecture, web technology, distributed computing, formal languages and an 18-EC final project. The route shown includes compiler construction and cryptography.

audience.programmeDescription: Computing Science at the University of Amsterdam develops programming, algorithms, mathematics and computer systems through courses and practical projects.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR option gives more weight to software, systems and algorithm design. The second applies computing and mathematics to signals, robotics and intelligent systems.
